reason: Rain can collect in hollows in the volcanic rock, a natural first step toward a sea.
expectation: The rain will gather into pools in the hollows.

effect: Rain has collected in pools, which can now move toward the basin.
reaction: The pools are a satisfying first sign of water accumulating.
reason: The slope suggests a route for the pooled water toward the broad basin.

choice.with: A slope toward a broad basin

expectation: Water will flow downhill toward the basin.

effect: The pools overflow into runoff, connecting low places on the way toward the basin.
reaction: The downhill flow follows naturally from the landscape.
reason: The runoff is the clearest lead toward the sea, but its next partner is not obvious.
expectation: Inspection should reveal how the runoff can gather or interact with the rock.

effect: Runoff can combine with either the hollows or the cracked crust, offering routes toward both goals.
reaction: The two options clarify the next choices.
reason: The hollows are a plausible place for runoff to collect into a larger body of water.
expectation: Runoff will accumulate in the low ground toward a sea.

alternatives.reason: This may instead reveal a route for water through the rock.

effect: Runoff has joined the basins into an early sea, completing the first goal.
reaction: It's satisfying to see the pools become a connected sea.
reason: Inspection showed that runoff can also combine with the cracked crust, suggesting a route through the rock.
expectation: Some runoff will enter fractures in the crust.

effect: Runoff enters fractures in the crust, revealing an underground route; the less permeable layer may shape where it goes next.
reaction: The contrast between surface runoff and hidden water is interesting.
reason: Water moving through fractured rock may collect or flow along the less permeable layer.
expectation: The layer will redirect or retain the water underground.

effect: The less permeable layer diverts groundwater sideways, suggesting it may emerge elsewhere.
reaction: The layer's effect makes the underground route clearer.
reason: The diverted groundwater is the clearest lead for completing the route through the rock, but its next partner is not obvious.
expectation: Inspection should reveal how the groundwater continues or reappears.

effect: The inspection automatically completed the groundwater route: water emerged as a spring on the slope, completing the remaining goal.
reaction: Seeing the hidden flow return to the surface was satisfying.

mostWorthwhile.text: Following runoff through fractured rock, along a less permeable layer and back out as a spring made the groundwater route understandable.

leastWorthwhile.text: Inspecting the runoff interrupted the flow a little, although it usefully revealed both possible routes.

surprise.text: The less permeable layer diverted groundwater sideways rather than simply stopping it, allowing it to reappear elsewhere.

arbitrary.text: Nothing felt particularly arbitrary; the combinations followed the landscape and water's movement.

continue.text: Yes. I would be curious to see how the new sea and shoreline change, especially if the next chapter connects those changes to natural processes as clearly as the groundwater route did.
